read: full: abstract and introduction (pp. 1-3), the dataset (pp. 3-4), accuracy evaluation (pp. 4-8), consistency evaluation (pp. 8-12), reasoning behaviours (pp. 12-20), conclusion and future work (pp. 20-21); references skimmed
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2408.08302v1, 15 Aug 2024, marked 'Preprint submitted to Transportation Research Part C' (p. 1); no published venue in the text
what_it_is: TransportBench is a set of 140 undergraduate transportation-engineering problems over ten topics, from transportation economics and traffic flow to public transit systems; 73 are true/false and the rest general Q&A (p. 3). The sixth author selected them from two of his University of Illinois courses (CEE 310 and CEE 418) and 'twisted' them from course problems and a co-authored textbook, replacing figures with text; each problem comes with a step-by-step LaTeX solution (pp. 3-4). Seven LLMs answered zero-shot through web interfaces. Human annotators judged correctness and also checked the models' reasoning (pp. 4-5). The paper adds consistency tests on the true/false problems (five independent trials, and answer flips under a self-check prompt) and case studies of reasoning errors (pp. 8-20).
size: 140 problems: 73 true/false and 67 general Q&A, going by the topic rows of Table 1 and by Table 3 (Table 1's total row prints 68 general Q&A against a total of 140) (pp. 3, 7); 7 LLMs: GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3 Opus, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5 Pro, Llama 3 70B and Llama 3.1 405B (p. 5)
source_of_items: course material: problems adapted by the course instructor from two University of Illinois courses and a co-authored textbook (pp. 3-4)
has_gold_traces: partial: a detailed step-by-step LaTeX solution for each problem (p. 4), serving as the reference for human grading, not for automated scoring of steps
evaluation: human annotation of final-answer correctness (accuracy), with the models' reasoning also checked (p. 5); consistency measured on the 73 true/false problems by the mixed-response rate over five zero-shot trials and by answer flips under self-check prompts (pp. 9, 12); qualitative case studies of reasoning (pp. 12-20)
human_validation: All grading is by human annotation (p. 5). The course instructor chose the problems, and the second author prepared most solutions (pp. 3-4). The number of graders and their agreement are not reported.
contamination_measures: none stated; problems are adapted ('twisted') from course and textbook material rather than copied, but the paper does not present this as a contamination control (pp. 3-4)

engtrace_use.sentence: S-E1 (L182-190): '... while specialized benchmarks like TransportBench, APBench, and EEE-Bench (Syed et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Cheng et al., 2024; Li et al., 2025; Liu et al., 2025) are siloed within narrow sub-disciplines.'
engtrace_use.explanation: TransportBench is confined to transportation systems engineering, 'a critical interdisciplinary subfield of civil engineering' (p. 1), and is drawn from two courses (p. 3). So 'siloed within a narrow sub-discipline' holds, and the name TransportBench is the paper's own (p. 1). Caveat for the paragraph's closing generalisation, which rests on these citations (L199-201: 'existing benchmarks remain limited to outcome matching and fail to validate the physically grounded reasoning'). The scoring metric here is final-answer accuracy. But every problem has a step-by-step reference solution (p. 4), the human graders also checked the models' reasoning (p. 5), and the paper documents correct final answers reached through flawed reasoning (Problems 10.55 and 10.16, pp. 16-18). Counting that generalisation, the verdict would be imprecise.

suggested_wording: TransportBench (Syed et al., 2024) pairs 140 undergraduate transportation-engineering problems with step-by-step reference solutions, but scores models on human-judged final answers and examines their reasoning only in case studies.
facts_to_cite: 140 undergraduate transportation-engineering problems over ten topics, 73 of them true/false (p. 3)
selected by the course instructor from two University of Illinois courses and adapted from course problems and a co-authored textbook, with figures replaced by text (pp. 3-4)
each problem comes with a detailed step-by-step LaTeX solution (p. 4)
seven LLMs evaluated zero-shot, with correctness judged by human annotation; Claude 3.5 Sonnet was best at 67.1% (94/140) (pp. 5-6)
consistency tested over five trials and under self-check prompts on the 73 true/false problems (pp. 9, 12)
case studies show correct final answers reached through flawed reasoning (pp. 16-18)
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: engineering domain (civil, though transportation is not among EngTrace's civil domains); a step-by-step reference solution per problem; human-expert grading; attention to correct answers reached by flawed reasoning; and consistency over repeated trials. Lacks: generated instances (140 fixed problems); automated step-level evaluation (reasoning is examined only in case studies); a validated automated evaluator; and coverage beyond one sub-discipline.
notes: Table 1 is internally inconsistent: its topic rows sum to 67 general Q&A problems, but its total row prints 68 alongside a total of 140; Table 3 uses 67 (pp. 3, 7). Its section 5.2, 'Correct final answers may come from flawed reasoning approaches' (p. 16), is a direct precedent for EngTrace's motivation (right answer, wrong step), so the revision should credit it rather than fold it into 'outcome matching'.
